display_title: Do Trading Signals Beat Buy-and-Hold? A Backtest and a Live Alerting Pipeline
one_liner: An eight-strategy, 19-year backtest of the technical signals behind a self-built Raspberry Pi alerting pipeline. No signal beat buy-and-hold on return, and a published trend filter cut drawdown by more than half.
problem: A long-horizon, tax-sheltered account must choose between passive buy-and-hold and tactical rules (trend filters, momentum, oscillator signals). Popular signals are widely promoted, but whether they improve risk-adjusted outcomes after costs is an empirical question.
approach: I wrote a vectorized daily engine that applies each strategy's target weights to adjusted ETF prices (SPY, EFA, IEF, GSG, VNQ, AGG, with BIL as cash) from May 2007 to May 2026. Every strategy shares the same dates, cost model of 1 bp per side, and cash proxy, and is scored on CAGR, volatility, Sharpe, Sortino, maximum drawdown, Calmar and turnover against buy-and-hold SPY. The signals come from HedgeAbove, a cron-driven rule engine I run on a Raspberry Pi with SQLite deduplication, Telegram delivery, point-in-time SEC EDGAR fundamentals and walk-forward threshold selection.
decision_relevance: Frames an allocation choice as decision analysis under uncertainty: state the criterion, which here is drawdown and risk-adjusted return rather than raw CAGR, test the alternatives on equal terms, and accept the answer the data gives.

headline_results.claim: Eight strategies backtested over 19 years (2007-2026) at 1 bp costs: none beat buy-and-hold SPY on return (10.68% CAGR)
The Faber 200-day moving-average filter cut maximum drawdown from -55.2% to -24.6% while keeping 90% of the return (9.59% CAGR)
Faber Sharpe 0.65 against 0.51 for buy-and-hold, a difference that does not clear a block-bootstrap interval of [-0.21, +0.49]. The drawdown reduction is the durable finding, not the return
Oscillator signals underperformed: RSI mean reversion Sharpe 0.11, MACD cross 0.43 at 42x annual turnover
The live alerting pipeline runs on point-in-time SEC EDGAR fundamentals, filtered to filing date so no signal sees data before it was public

limitations: A single 19-year sample dominated by one major bear market (2008-09) and a short one (2020); no 1970s-style inflation regime.
Trades fill at the same close that generates the signal. With next-day execution, Faber's Sharpe falls from 0.65 to 0.59 and its CAGR from 9.59% to 8.80%.
Trend and momentum strategies sit in cash during their 200-252 day warm-up (May 2007 to mid-2008), which flatters them. Over a common post-warm-up window the Sharpe edge shrinks from +0.14 to +0.09.
Eight strategies were compared without a multiple-testing adjustment.
Static weights are effectively rebalanced daily at zero cost. Only 1 bp costs are tested. No slippage model.
yfinance adjusted prices are revised after the fact, and the data vintage is not committed.
Educational research only, not investment advice.
blockers_before_featuring: OWNER DECISION: roth-backtest (the analytic core) is private and has no remote. Make it public or move the analysis into public HedgeAbove
HedgeAbove now has no published quantitative evidence by design; an exploratory result with episode counts and CIs needs a network run plus committed artifacts
No saved record of fired alerts and forward outcomes, so this stays a research entry rather than a product one
Removed subscription marketing remains in the public git history (JER question is a human call)
Cite a specific SPIVA scorecard year/table or drop the reference
caveat: A personal research project, not investment advice.
